title: The UK childhood immunisation schedule and herd immunity
blurb: Apply the UKHSA routine schedule from 1 September 2026, explain how vaccines and population immunity work, and handle common checks such as SCID screening.
question: A baby attends at 12 weeks for routine immunisations in October 2026. Her mother asks which vaccines are due today, which are due next time, and why vaccinating her baby also protects others. How should the nurse answer?

teach.body: Vaccines produce active immunity: the child's own immune system makes antibodies and immunological memory, without the risks of the disease. Passive immunity (antibodies crossing the placenta, or immunoglobulin) is temporary, lasting weeks to months. Plain English: a vaccine teaches the body to recognise the germ, so it can fight it off quickly later.

head: Age
Vaccines
rows: dTaP/IPV (plus MMRV if born by 31 Dec 2024)
HPV, single dose, boys and girls
teach.caption: *18-month appointment for children born on or after 1 July 2024. 6-in-1 = DTaP/IPV/Hib/HepB. Annual nasal flu (LAIV) from age 2 through school years.

teach.text: The 2026 schedule moved things: MenB is at 8 AND 12 weeks (not 16), PCV is at 16 weeks, and MMR is now MMRV (with varicella). Older 'Hib/MenC at 12 months' and 'MMR at 3 years 4 months' answers are wrong for younger cohorts.

teach.caption: If nasal LAIV is contraindicated or unsuitable, give inactivated flu vaccine instead. LAIV contains porcine gelatine.

teach.body: Vaccinated people are less likely to pass infection on, so people who cannot be vaccinated (too young, or immunosuppressed) are protected too. Example from the Green Book: vaccinating teenagers with MenACWY reduces carriage and protects babies who are not routinely given MenC. High coverage can eliminate a disease; if coverage falls, it can return.
teach.cite: UKHSA Green Book Chapter 1, Population immunity

steps.label: Result missing
steps.sub: Do not give yet; give the other vaccines and chase it

teach.caption: SCID = severe combined immunodeficiency. Live vaccines can cause serious infection in severely immunocompromised babies.

items: Hana, 12 weeks, attends for her second set of immunisations in October 2026.
Nurse Ade checks the red book: 8-week vaccines given, SCID screening result recorded and clear.
He gives the 6-in-1 and MenB into the thigh, and oral rotavirus. He explains PCV and the third 6-in-1 are due at 16 weeks.
He explains population immunity to Hana's mother: high coverage also protects babies too young to be vaccinated.

BCG within 28 days of birth for at-risk infants

items: 8 weeks: 6-in-1, MenB, rotavirus. 12 weeks: 6-in-1, MenB, rotavirus. 16 weeks: 6-in-1, PCV.
1 year: PCV, MenB boosters and MMRV; 18 months: 6-in-1 and MMRV (born from 1 July 2024).
HPV single dose at 12-13; Td/IPV and MenACWY at 14.
Check SCID screening before rotavirus and BCG.
Population immunity protects those who cannot be vaccinated.

summary: You can now state the UKHSA routine schedule from 1 September 2026, explain active, passive and population immunity, distinguish live from inactivated vaccines, and apply safety checks such as the SCID screening result before rotavirus.

A.q: Sofia, 8 weeks, attends for her first routine immunisations in England in October 2026. Which vaccines should she be offered?
A.why: At 8 weeks the schedule from 1 September 2026 gives the 6-in-1 (DTaP/IPV/Hib/HepB), MenB and oral rotavirus.

whyNot.0: PCV is given at 16 weeks, not 8 weeks.
whyNot.2: PCV is not due at 8 weeks, and rotavirus is.
whyNot.3: MenB is also due at 8 weeks.

A.q: Ali, 16 weeks, attends for his third set of routine immunisations. Which vaccines are due?
A.why: At 16 weeks the schedule gives the third 6-in-1 and PCV.

whyNot.0: MenB is given at 8 and 12 weeks in the 2026 schedule, not 16.
whyNot.1: Rotavirus is given at 8 and 12 weeks only, and MenB is not due at 16 weeks.
whyNot.2: The third 6-in-1 is due at 16 weeks; MenB is not.

A.q: Which statement best describes population (herd) immunity?
options: Vaccinating many people protects those who cannot be vaccinated
Antibodies cross the placenta to protect the newborn
Natural infection gives longer protection than vaccines
Each vaccinated person is fully protected for life
A.why: Vaccinated people are less likely to be a source of infection, so unvaccinated individuals are less likely to be exposed (Green Book Chapter 1).

whyNot.2: This does not describe population immunity; vaccines give immunity similar to infection without its risks.
whyNot.3: This describes individual protection, and protection varies by vaccine.

B.q: Jacob has his first birthday next week. Which vaccines are due at his 1-year appointment?
options: Hib/MenC booster, PCV booster and MMR
PCV booster, MenB booster and MMRV
MenB booster and first MMR dose
B.why: On or after the first birthday: PCV booster, MenB booster and MMRV.

whyNot.0: Hib/MenC and MMR at 1 year belong to the older schedule.
whyNot.1: The 4th 6-in-1 and second MMRV are given at 18 months.
whyNot.3: PCV is also due, and MMR has been replaced by MMRV.

B.q: Ellie, 8 weeks, is due her first immunisations. Her SCID newborn screening result is not in her record. What should the nurse do?
options: Give all three as the result is likely normal
Postpone all vaccines until the result is found
Give rotavirus and hold the injected vaccines
B.why: The schedule states rotavirus should only be given after checking the SCID screening result, because it is a live vaccine. Inactivated vaccines need not be delayed.

whyNot.1: The result must be checked first; a live vaccine could harm a baby with SCID.
whyNot.2: There is no reason to delay the inactivated vaccines.
whyNot.3: This reverses the risk: rotavirus is the live vaccine that needs the check.

B.q: Grace was born in September 2024. Her mother asks why Grace has an 18-month appointment when her older son, born in March 2024, did not. What is the reason?
options: Grace was born preterm and needs extra doses
Her son missed his appointment and needs catch-up
The change applies to children born from 2025
Children born on or after 1 July 2024 have it
B.why: The 18-month appointment (6-in-1 4th dose and MMRV) applies to children born on or after 1 July 2024; those born on or before 30 June 2024 have no 18-month appointment.

whyNot.0: The appointment depends on date of birth, not prematurity.
whyNot.1: Her son was not due an 18-month appointment.
whyNot.2: The cut-off is births on or after 1 July 2024, not 2025, so Grace qualifies.

C.q: Ava, 4, is receiving chemotherapy and is severely immunosuppressed. Her parents ask about her annual flu vaccine, usually given as a nasal spray. What should the nurse advise?
options: Give the nasal spray as usual
Delay all flu vaccination until treatment ends
Give the nasal spray at half the dose
C.why: The nasal spray (LAIV) is a live vaccine. If LAIV is contraindicated or unsuitable, inactivated flu vaccine is given; household members and carers may also be offered flu vaccine.

whyNot.0: A live vaccine is unsuitable in severe immunosuppression.
whyNot.2: She is at high risk from flu, so protection should not be withheld.
whyNot.3: Halving the dose does not remove the risk of a live vaccine.

C.q: Oliver, 14 and in Year 9, attends a school immunisation session. His record shows one dose of MMR. Which plan is correct?
options: Td/IPV and MenACWY; no action on MMR
HPV and MenACWY; MMR not needed at 14
Td/IPV and MenACWY, and offer a second MMR
Td/IPV now; MenACWY is given at 18
C.why: At 14 (Year 9) Td/IPV and MenACWY are given and MMR status is checked; a missing second dose should be offered.

whyNot.0: The schedule says to check MMR status at this visit and act on gaps.
whyNot.1: HPV is given at 12-13, and incomplete MMR should be addressed.
whyNot.3: MenACWY is given at 14 in Year 9.

C.q: A mother asks why her baby is not given MenC, but her teenager is given MenACWY at school. Which explanation is correct?
options: Teen vaccination cuts spread and protects babies
MenC is given at 3 years 4 months instead
Babies get MenC protection from breast milk
MenC disease does not occur in babies
C.why: The Green Book explains that vaccinating teenagers, who have the highest carriage rates, reduces transmission and protects infants: population immunity.

whyNot.1: MenC is not part of the 3 years 4 months appointment.
whyNot.2: Breast milk is not the reason babies are protected against MenC.
whyNot.3: Babies can get meningococcal C disease; they are protected through population immunity.

reteach.title: A wall around the baby
reteach.question: How can a teenager's vaccine protect a newborn?

blocks.body: Germs need people to pass between. Each vaccinated person is a closed door. When enough doors close, the germ cannot reach those who are too young or too unwell to be vaccinated. That is population immunity, and why high coverage matters.

blocks.text: MenB: 8 and 12 weeks. PCV: 16 weeks. Both boosted at 1 year.

explain.body: Active immunity is made by the person's own immune system, by infection or vaccination, and is long-lasting. Passive immunity comes from transferred antibodies (placenta, immunoglobulin) and lasts weeks to months.

test.q: A newborn is protected against measles for a few months by antibodies from her mother. What type of immunity is this?
test.why: Antibodies transferred across the placenta give temporary passive immunity.

whyNot.0: Active immunity is produced by the baby's own immune system after infection.
whyNot.1: Vaccination produces active acquired immunity in the person vaccinated.
whyNot.2: Population immunity comes from high vaccine coverage in others.

explain.body: 8 weeks: 6-in-1, MenB, rotavirus. 12 weeks: 6-in-1, MenB, rotavirus. 16 weeks: 6-in-1, PCV. Injections into the thigh in infants.

test.q: At which ages is MenB given in the infant primary schedule from 1 September 2026?
test.why: From 1 September 2026, MenB is given at 8 and 12 weeks, with a booster at 1 year.

whyNot.0: 16 weeks was MenB's slot in older schedules; it is now PCV.
whyNot.3: MenB primary doses are at 8 and 12 weeks; 1 year is the booster.

explain.body: 1 year: PCV, MenB boosters and MMRV. 18 months (born from 1 July 2024): 6-in-1 and MMRV. 3 years 4 months: dTaP/IPV. 12-13: HPV single dose. 14: Td/IPV and MenACWY. Annual nasal flu from 2.

test.q: How many doses of HPV vaccine are routinely given at 12 to 13 years?
test.why: HPV (Gardasil 9) is given as a single dose to boys and girls aged 12-13.

whyNot.0: Three doses belong to older schedules.
whyNot.1: Two doses were used before the move to a single dose.
whyNot.3: Four doses have not been used for HPV in the routine programme.

explain.body: Rotavirus and BCG are given only after checking the SCID screening result. Live vaccines such as LAIV are unsuitable in severe immunosuppression; inactivated alternatives are used.

test.q: Which routine infant vaccine needs the SCID screening result checked before it is given?
test.why: Rotavirus is a live oral vaccine; the schedule says give it only after checking the SCID screening result.

whyNot.1: MenB is not live and does not need the SCID check.
